extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in a first-semester real analysis / advanced calculus course
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, counterexamples, and sufficient conditions for interchanging limits (pointwise vs uniform convergence) in sequences of functions: continuity, integration, differentiation, and power-series termwise operations; plus Picard's theorem for ODE existence/uniqueness and its Picard-iteration proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence preserves continuity (Theorem 6.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (f_n) is a sequence of continuous functions on S and f_n converges uniformly to f on S, then f is continuous on S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the ε-triangle-inequality trick: fix ε, pick K so sup_x |f_k(x)-f(x)| < ε/3, use continuity of f_k at the point, and combine. Anti-pattern: pointwise convergence need not preserve continuity (see Example 6.2.1 where pointwise limit is discontinuous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence allows interchange of limit and integral (Theorem 6.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f_n are Riemann integrable on [a,b] and f_n → f uniformly on [a,b], then f is Riemann integrable and ∫_a^b f = lim_{n→∞} ∫_a^b f_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof bounds the integral of the difference by sup_x |f_n(x)-f(x)| times interval length and uses integrability of each f_n. Anti-pattern/example: merely pointwise convergence can fail to interchange limits and integrals (Example 6.2.3). The text notes weaker Lebesgue-type hypotheses (dominated convergence) give more general theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence of derivatives needed to pass limit inside derivative (Theorem 6.2.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a bounded interval I, if (f_n) are continuously differentiable on I, f_n converge uniformly to f on I, and the derivatives f_n' converge uniformly to a function g on I (and f_n(c) converges for some c∈I), then f is differentiable and f' = g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the fundamental theorem of calculus and uniform convergence of the derivative sequence to interchange integration and limit. Anti-patterns: uniform convergence of f_n alone is insufficient (Examples 6.2.8 and 6.2.9 show derivatives need not converge or need not converge uniformly; pointwise convergence of derivatives isn't enough).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pointwise convergence does not preserve key properties (pitfalls and counterexamples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pointwise convergence alone does not guarantee continuity, integrability (Riemann), boundedness, or that limits commute with integrals/derivatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative counterexamples in the text: Example 6.2.1 (sequence of continuous functions with pointwise limit discontinuous), Example 6.2.3 (pointwise limit zero but integrals not tending to integral of limit), Example 6.2.6 (pointwise limit is Dirichlet function, not Riemann integrable), Example 6.2.7 (pointwise limit of bounded functions can be unbounded). Use these to check hypotheses before swapping limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence of a power series on compact subintervals (Proposition 6.2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: A power series ∑ c_n (x-a)^n has radius of convergence ρ>0; for any 0<r<ρ the series converges uniformly on the closed interval [a-r,a+r]; hence the sum is continuous there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: pick r<ρ so ∑ |c_n| r^n converges; then the tail of the power series is uniformly small on |x-a|≤r by comparison. Consequence: inside radius of convergence one has uniform convergence on each closed subinterval, enabling termwise operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term-by-term integration and differentiation of power series (Corollaries 6.2.12 and 6.2.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a power series with radius ρ, one may integrate it term-by-term to obtain a series with radius at least ρ (Cor. 6.2.12). One may differentiate it term-by-term; the differentiated series has the same radius of convergence ρ and gives the derivative of the sum (Cor. 6.2.13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rely on uniform convergence on |x-a|≤r for r<ρ and Theorem 6.2.10 for differentiation. Guidance: choose r<ρ, justify uniform convergence of partial sums and of differentiated partial sums, then pass limits under integral/differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence on compact subsets (compact-uniform convergence) preserves continuity and integrability on each compact (exercise 6.2.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f_n are continuous on ℝ and converge uniformly on every compact subset to f, then f is continuous; if f_n are Riemann integrable on every closed bounded interval and converge uniformly on compact subsets to f, then for every [a,b] we can interchange limit and integral on [a,b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the natural extension of uniform convergence on a single compact interval to families of compacts; use the result on each fixed closed bounded interval. Helpful when handling functions on unbounded domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dini's theorem (monotone pointwise convergence implies uniform on compact interval) (exercise 6.2.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (f_n) is a monotone sequence of continuous functions on [a,b] (e.g., f_1 ≥ f_2 ≥ ... ≥ 0) that converges pointwise to 0 on [a,b], then convergence is uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supplies a useful sufficient condition for upgrading pointwise to uniform convergence: monotonicity + continuity on a compact interval. Use when monotone structure is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationships between convergence modes and L1-norm (exercises 6.2.8–6.2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: The L1-norm (∥f∥_{L1} = ∫_0^1 |f|) yields another notion of convergence: L1-convergence. Uniform convergence of integrable functions implies L1 convergence to zero; pointwise convergence does not imply convergence in L1 (examples exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use L1 when uniform convergence is too strong; be aware of examples where pointwise convergence gives no control of integrals (so L1 limit may fail to exist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint vs iterated limits for double sequences (exercises 6.2.13–6.2.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint limit lim_{n,m→∞} x_{n,m} = L (in the two-parameter sense) does not automatically guarantee that the iterated limits lim_{n→∞} (lim_{m→∞} x_{n,m}) or lim_{m→∞} (lim_{n→∞} x_{n,m}) exist or equal L; conversely, existence of iterated limits separately does not guarantee the joint limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexamples are given; to interchange or pass limits in double sequences or double-indexed functions one needs uniformity-type hypotheses or dominant bounds. Use the definition of joint limit (ε–M) and uniform Cauchy arguments to check interchangeability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard's theorem: existence and uniqueness for ODE y' = F(x,y) (Theorem 6.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let I and J be intervals and (x0,y0) in interior(I)×interior(J). If F(x,y) is continuous on a closed bounded rectangle and Lipschitz in y (there is L with |F(x,y)-F(x,z)| ≤ L|y-z| for all x in I, y,z in J), then there exists h>0 and a unique differentiable function f on [x0-h,x0+h] solving f'(x)=F(x,f(x)) with f(x0)=y0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive proof via Picard iteration: pick M bounding F, choose α (and hence h) so that the Picard operator is a contraction (essentially L*h<1), define iterates f_{k+1}(x)=y0+∫_{x0}^x F(t,f_k(t)) dt, show uniform convergence to solution, and prove uniqueness using the contraction/supremum argument. The theorem gives local existence; by uniqueness one can glue local solutions to extend as permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard iteration as a constructive approximation method
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the contraction condition (small enough h so Lipschitz constant times interval length <1) the Picard iterates f_0, f_1, ... defined by f_0≡y0 and f_{k+1}(x)=y0+∫_{x0}^x F(t,f_k(t)) dt converge uniformly to the unique solution; error bounds decay geometrically with the contraction constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bounds sup |f_{k+1}-f_k| ≤ C^k sup |f_1-f_0| with C<1 to show uniform Cauchy property. Practical guidance: compute L and bound M to choose working h; the proof yields explicit iterative approximations to approximate the solution numerically or analytically.
